{祝贺|zhù hè} (to congratulate) is lesson 05's word.

## Pronunciation

- {赢|yíng} yíng and {应|yīng} yīng ({应该|yīng gāi}): the same syllable, second and first tones. {输|shū} shū and {书|shū} shū are
  homophones.
- {奖|jiǎng} jiǎng and {讲|jiǎng} jiǎng (to speak, {演讲|yǎn jiǎng}) are homophones too; {奖金|jiǎng jīn} jiǎng jīn has a third tone, then a
  first.
- {队|duì} duì and {对|duì} duì (right, correct) are homophones: {队员|duì yuán} duì yuán.
- {鼓励|gǔ lì} gǔ lì: a dipping tone, then a falling one. {获得|huò dé} huò dé: two tones that fall and rise, 4+2.
- {不光|bù guāng} bù guāng: {不|bù} keeps its fourth tone before a first-tone syllable; {不仅|bù jǐn} bù jǐn before a third.
- {场|chǎng} is chǎng here ({一|yì}{场|chǎng}{比赛|bǐ sài}), third tone, as in {操场|cāo chǎng} and {市场|shì chǎng} (a market, lesson 09).

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{输|shū}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}~~: {输|shū} is to lose a game. Losing a thing is {丢|diū}: {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{手机|shǒu jī}{丢|diū}{了|le}.
- ~~{他|tā}{不仅|bù jǐn}{会|huì}{唱歌|chàng gē}，{不仅|bù jǐn}{会|huì}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}~~: the second clause takes {还|hái}, {而且|ér qiě} or {也|yě}: {他|tā}{不仅|bù jǐn}{会|huì}{唱歌|chàng gē}，{还|hái}{会|huì}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}.
- ~~{不仅|bù jǐn}{他|tā}{会|huì}{唱歌|chàng gē}，{还|hái}{会|huì}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}~~ with one subject: the subject comes before {不仅|bù jǐn}: {他|tā}{不仅|bù jǐn}{会|huì}{唱歌|chàng gē}…
- ~~{老师|lǎo shī}{并且|bìng qiě}{学生|xué sheng}~~: {并且|bìng qiě} joins verbs and clauses, not nouns: {老师|lǎo shī}{和|hé}{学生|xué sheng}.
- {赢|yíng}{了|le}{第一名|dì yī míng} is heard, but the usual verbs for a place or a prize are {得|dé} and {获得|huò dé}: {他|tā}{获得|huò dé}{了|le}{第一名|dì yī míng} /
  {他|tā}{得|dé}{了|le}{第一名|dì yī míng}.
- {一|yí}{个|gè}{比赛|bǐ sài} is heard in speech; the measure word to learn is {场|chǎng}: {一|yì}{场|chǎng}{比赛|bǐ sài}. An event in a list is
  {一|yí}{项|xiàng}.

## Key points

- {不仅|bù jǐn} / {不光|bù guāng} (spoken) …{还|hái} / {而且|ér qiě} / {也|yě}: not only… but also. One subject goes first; with two, {不仅|bù jǐn}
  comes before the first and the second clause has {也|yě}.
- {并且|bìng qiě}: and also, moreover (verbs and clauses, not nouns). {另外|lìng wài} / {此外|cǐ wài}: in addition; {另外|lìng wài} + number or
  noun: the other(s). {加上|jiā shàng}: on top of that.
- {举办|jǔ bàn}: someone organises an event; {举行|jǔ xíng}: an event takes place ({在|zài}…{举行|jǔ xíng}).
- {赢|yíng} (a game), {赢得|yíng dé} (praise, support), {输|shū} (a game), {打败|dǎ bài} + opponent, {获得|huò dé} (a prize, a place: formal),
  {获奖|huò jiǎng}, {奖|jiǎng}, {奖金|jiǎng jīn}.
- {鼓励|gǔ lì} / {邀请|yāo qǐng} + person + verb; {表扬|biǎo yáng} (praise), {庆祝|qìng zhù} (celebrate).
- {一|yì}{场|chǎng}{比赛|bǐ sài} (a match, a show), {一|yí}{项|xiàng}{活动|huó dòng} (an item, an event).
- New characters (simplified): {={资|zī}、{品|pǐn}、{阅|yuè}、{扬|yáng}、{棒|bàng}、{光|guāng}、{并|bìng}、{仅|jǐn}、{队|duì}、{败|bài}、{鼓|gǔ}、{励|lì}、{喊|hǎn}、{奖|jiǎng}、{金|jīn}、{获|huò}、{另|lìng}、{排|pái}、{庆|qìng}、{祝|zhù}=}; eleven differ in traditional.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Graduation and what comes next: not this but that
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

It's June, and {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (Wang Fang) and {李明|Lǐ Míng} (Li Ming) are graduating. {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī} (Teacher Wang) writes
them a letter; {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) comes to congratulate them; and everyone talks about what comes next. {李明|Lǐ Míng}
is going to Britain in September for a master's degree. This lesson gives you the words of plans, dreams,
further study, success and failure, and four pieces of grammar:

- {不|bú}{是|shì}…{而是|ér shì}…: not A, but B (a **[[correction]]**), beside {不|bú}{是|shì}…{就是|jiù shì}… (either A or B);
- {将|jiāng} and {将要|jiāng yào}: "will, be going to" in written Chinese;
- {而|ér}: "and, but, while" in written Chinese;
- {一切|yí qiè}: everything, all.

You also learn {祝|zhù} (to wish) and {祝贺|zhù hè} (to congratulate), which are easy to mix up.

## {不|bú}{是|shì}…{而是|ér shì}…: not A, but B

{不|bú}{是|shì} A ，{而是|ér shì} B corrects a wrong idea: it isn't A, it's B. Often the speaker is answering what
someone else thinks:

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{而是|ér shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}。 — It isn't that I don't want to go: I don't have time.

{他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}，{而是|ér shì}{日本|Rì běn}{人|rén}。 — He isn't Chinese, he's Japanese.

{我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{为了|wèi le}{考试|kǎo shì}，{而是|ér shì}{因为|yīn wèi}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。 — I'm not learning Chinese for the exams but because
I enjoy it.

- {而是|ér shì} counts as one unit here; {是|shì} is the verb "to be", and {而|ér} marks the contrast. In relaxed speech
  people often drop {而|ér}: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{是|shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān} (lesson 03's dialogue had this).
- The two halves are usually parallel: two nouns, two reasons, two actions.
- {不|bú}{是|shì} A ，{而是|ér shì} B is the opposite order of "B, not A": {他|tā}{是|shì}{日本|Rì běn}{人|rén}，{不|bú}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén} says the same thing
  more plainly.

Don't confuse it with **{不|bú}{是|shì}…{就是|jiù shì}…**, which lists the only two possibilities: "if it isn't A, it's
B", "either A or B".

{周末|zhōu mò}{他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{看|kàn}{书|shū}，{就是|jiù shì}{上网|shàng wǎng}。 — At weekends he's either reading or online.

{这|zhè}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}{不|bú}{是|shì}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{就是|jiù shì}{刮风|guā fēng}。 — These last few days it's been either raining or windy. ({刮风|guā fēng}:
to be windy)

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {不|bú}{是|shì} A ，{而是|ér shì} B | not A, but B (correcting) | {不|bú}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{而是|ér shì}{太|tài}{忙|máng}{了|le}。 |
| {不|bú}{是|shì} A ，{就是|jiù shì} B | either A or B (only these two) | {他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{在|zài}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}，{就是|jiù shì}{在|zài}{食堂|shí táng}。 He's either in the library or the canteen. |

## {将|jiāng} and {将要|jiāng yào}: will, be going to (written)

{将|jiāng} + verb is the written way to talk about the future, the {会|huì} or {要|yào} of notices, news, letters and
speeches. {将要|jiāng yào} stresses that it will happen soon, like {快要|kuài yào}:

{毕业|bì yè}{典礼|diǎn lǐ}{将|jiāng}{在|zài}{六|liù}{月|yuè}{二十|èr shí}{日|rì}{举行|jǔ xíng}。 — The graduation ceremony will be held on 20 June. ({典礼|diǎn lǐ}: a
ceremony)

{你们|nǐ men}{将要|jiāng yào}{离开|lí kāi}{学校|xué xiào}{了|le}。 — You'll soon be leaving the university.

{明天|míng tiān}{将|jiāng}{有|yǒu}{大|dà}{雨|yǔ}。 — There will be heavy rain tomorrow. (a weather forecast)

In a chat, the same sentences would use {会|huì}, {要|yào} or {快要|kuài yào}…{了|le}: {我们|wǒ men}{快要|kuài yào}{毕业|bì yè}{了|le}。 (We're about to
graduate.) You'll meet {将|jiāng} again in lesson 13 in another written job: standing in for {把|bǎ} ({请|qǐng}{将|jiāng}{表格|biǎo gé}{填写|tián xiě}
{完整|wán zhěng}, please fill in the form). The meaning there is different; the context tells you which it is.

Two words for the future come with it:

- {将来|jiāng lái} is "the future, in future", the longer view: {我|wǒ}{将来|jiāng lái}{想|xiǎng}{当|dāng}{老师|lǎo shī}。 (I'd like to be a teacher one
  day; {当|dāng}: to work as.) {将来|jiāng lái}{的|de}{计划|jì huà} (plans for the future).
- {今后|jīn hòu} is "from now on, from today": {今后|jīn hòu}{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{更加|gèng jiā}{努力|nǔ lì}。 (From now on I'll work even harder.)
  It starts at the present moment; {将来|jiāng lái} is somewhere ahead.

## {而|ér}: and, but, while (written)

{而|ér} is a written conjunction with two jobs.

**Contrast** ("while, whereas, but"), between two clauses that say different things about two
subjects:

{哥哥|gē ge}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{运动|yùn dòng}，{而|ér}{弟弟|dì di}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。 — My older brother likes sport, while my younger brother likes
reading.

{北方|běi fāng}{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{而|ér}{南方|nán fāng}{很|hěn}{暖和|nuǎn huo}。 — In the north winters are cold, whereas in the south they're
warm. ({暖和|nuǎn huo}: warm, lesson 26)

**Joining** two adjectives or verbs that go together ("and, yet"), in set phrases and careful
writing:

{这个|zhè ge}{方法|fāng fǎ}{简单|jiǎn dān}{而|ér}{有用|yǒu yòng}。 — The method is simple yet useful.

You know {而|ér} already inside other words: {而且|ér qiě} (HSK 3, moreover), {而是|ér shì} (above), and in lesson 14,
{然而|rán ér} (however). In speech the contrast is {可是|kě shì}, {但是|dàn shì} or just a pause; {而|ér} belongs in writing.

## {一切|yí qiè}: everything, all

{一切|yí qiè} stands for "everything, all of it", as a noun, or goes before a noun as "all":

{一切|yí qiè}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{顺利|shùn lì}。 — Everything went smoothly. ({顺利|shùn lì}: smooth, lesson 17)

{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}{为|wèi}{我|wǒ}{做|zuò}{的|de}{一切|yí qiè}。 — Thank you for everything you've done for me.

{一切|yí qiè}{问题|wèn tí}{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}{一起|yì qǐ}{解决|jiě jué}。 — We can solve all the problems together. ({解决|jiě jué}: to solve)

{祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{一切|yí qiè}{顺利|shùn lì}！ is the standard wish at a farewell or a new beginning: "all the best". {一切|yí qiè} is a
little more formal than "everything" in English; {所有|suǒ yǒu} (all, lesson 15) is the everyday word before a
noun ({所有|suǒ yǒu}{的|de}{人|rén}, everyone).

## Plans and dreams

- {计划|jì huà} is a plan and to plan: {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}{计划|jì huà}？ (What are your plans?) {我|wǒ}{计划|jì huà}{明年|míng nián}{去|qù}{英国|Yīng guó}。
- {目标|mù biāo} is a goal, a target you aim to reach: {我|wǒ}{的|de}{目标|mù biāo}{是|shì}{通过|tōng guò} HSK {四级|sì jí}。
- {目的|mù dì} is a purpose, the reason you do something: {我|wǒ}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{的|de}{目的|mù dì}{是|shì}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 (My purpose in coming
  to China is to learn Chinese.) {目标|mù biāo} is what you're heading for; {目的|mù dì} is why.
- {理想|lǐ xiǎng} is an ideal, and especially your dream for your future work: {我|wǒ}{的|de}{理想|lǐ xiǎng}{是|shì}{当|dāng}{一|yì}{名|míng}{记者|jì zhě}。 (My
  dream is to be a journalist; {记者|jì zhě}: lesson 24.) As an adjective, ideal: {这个|zhè ge}{地方|dì fang}{很|hěn}{理想|lǐ xiǎng}。
- {梦想|mèng xiǎng} is a dream you hope to realise, and "to dream of": {她|tā}{的|de}{梦想|mèng xiǎng}{是|shì}{去|qù}{世界|shì jiè}{各地|gè dì}{旅行|lǚ xíng}。 ({各地|gè dì}: everywhere; {旅行|lǚ xíng}: to travel, lesson 18) {梦|mèng} is a dream
  in your sleep ({做梦|zuò mèng}, to have a dream, lesson 20) and also a dream in the wider sense.
- {人生|rén shēng} is (a person's) life, life as a whole; {一生|yì shēng} is one's whole lifetime, all one's life: {他|tā}{的|de}{一生|yì shēng}
  {都|dōu}{在|zài}{教育|jiào yù}{学生|xué sheng}。 (He spent all his life teaching.) {教育|jiào yù} is education, and to educate.
- {美好|měi hǎo} is fine, happy, beautiful, for life, the future, memories: {美好|měi hǎo}{的|de}{将来|jiāng lái}, {美好|měi hǎo}{的|de}{回忆|huí yì} (fond
  memories).

## Further study

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {毕业|bì yè} | to graduate | {我|wǒ}{明年|míng nián}{大学|dà xué}{毕业|bì yè}。 I graduate from university next year. |
| {毕业生|bì yè shēng} | a graduate | {今年|jīn nián}{的|de}{毕业生|bì yè shēng} this year's graduates |
| {研究生|yán jiū shēng} | a postgraduate student | {读|dú}{研究生|yán jiū shēng} to do a postgraduate degree |
| {硕士|shuò shì} | a master's degree; a master's graduate | {读|dú}{硕士|shuò shì} to do a master's |
| {博士|bó shì} | a doctorate, PhD; a doctor (PhD holder) | {钱|Qián}{博士|bó shì} Dr Qian (a PhD, not a medical doctor) |
| {奖学金|jiǎng xué jīn} | a scholarship | {申请|shēn qǐng}{奖学金|jiǎng xué jīn} to apply for a scholarship |
| {申请|shēn qǐng} | to apply (for); an application | {申请|shēn qǐng}{去|qù}{英国|Yīng guó}{留学|liú xué} to apply to study in Britain |
| {报考|bào kǎo} | to apply to sit an entrance exam (for a school) | {报考|bào kǎo}{研究生|yán jiū shēng} to sit the postgraduate entrance exam |
| {高考|gāo kǎo} | the national college entrance exam | {高考|gāo kǎo}{是|shì}{每|měi}{年|nián}{六|liù}{月|yuè}。 The gaokao is every June. |
| {通过|tōng guò} | to pass (an exam); through, by means of | {通过|tōng guò}{考试|kǎo shì} pass an exam; {通过|tōng guò}{朋友|péng you}{认识|rèn shi} meet through a friend |

- {毕业|bì yè} is a separable verb: {毕|bì}{了|le}{业|yè} (graduated), {大学|dà xué}{毕业|bì yè} (graduate from university). It takes no
  object: ~~{毕业|bì yè}{大学|dà xué}~~ is wrong; say {大学|dà xué}{毕业|bì yè} or {从|cóng}{大学|dà xué}{毕业|bì yè}.
- {申请|shēn qǐng} takes what you apply for ({申请|shēn qǐng}{奖学金|jiǎng xué jīn}, {申请|shēn qǐng}{签证|qiān zhèng}, a visa: lesson 17) or a verb ({申请|shēn qǐng}{去|qù}{留学|liú xué}).
- {高考|gāo kǎo} is the national exam Chinese school-leavers take to enter university.
- {通过|tōng guò} as a preposition, "through, by way of", comes before the verb: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{通过|tōng guò}{网上|wǎng shàng}{的|de}{广告|guǎng gào}{找|zhǎo}{到|dào}{这|zhè}
  {个|gè}{工作|gōng zuò}{的|de}。 (I found this job through an ad online; {广告|guǎng gào}: lesson 11.)

## Success, failure and change

- {成功|chéng gōng} is to succeed and success: {他|tā}{成功|chéng gōng}{了|le}！{祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{成功|chéng gōng}！ (Good luck!)
- {失败|shī bài} is to fail and failure: {失败|shī bài}{了|le}{也|yě}{没关系|méi guān xi}。 The saying {失败|shī bài}{是|shì}{成功|chéng gōng}{之|zhī}{母|mǔ} is "failure is the mother of
  success" ({之|zhī} is a written {的|de}, lesson 21).
- {放弃|fàng qì} is to give up: {不|bú}{要|yào}{放弃|fàng qì}！ (Don't give up!) {他|tā}{放弃|fàng qì}{了|le}{这个|zhè ge}{机会|jī huì}。
- {继续|jì xù} is to continue, to go on: {继续|jì xù}{学习|xué xí} (go on studying), {休息|xiū xi}{一下|yí xià}{再|zài}{继续|jì xù}。
- {改变|gǎi biàn} is to change something (a plan, a habit, a life), or to change, as a noun: {改变|gǎi biàn}{计划|jì huà} (change the
  plan). {改|gǎi} (lesson 02) is the short, everyday verb; {改变|gǎi biàn} is about bigger, deeper changes. {变|biàn} (HSK 3) is
  for something changing by itself: {天气|tiān qì}{变|biàn}{了|le}。
- {成为|chéng wéi} is to become: {成为|chéng wéi}{一|yì}{名|míng}{记者|jì zhě} (become a journalist). {为|wéi} here is **wéi**, the written "to be";
  you'll meet it again in lesson 12.
- {考虑|kǎo lǜ} is to consider, to think something over: {让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{考虑|kǎo lǜ}{一下|yí xià}。 (Let me think about it.)

## {祝|zhù} and {祝贺|zhù hè}

Both are about good wishes, but at different times:

| | When | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {祝|zhù} | for the future: you wish someone something | {祝|zhù} + person + wish | {祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{生日|shēng rì}{快乐|kuài lè}！{祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{一切|yí qiè}{顺利|shùn lì}！ |
| {祝贺|zhù hè} | for something achieved: you congratulate | {祝贺|zhù hè} + person (+ what happened) | {祝贺|zhù hè}{你|nǐ}{毕业|bì yè}{了|le}！{祝贺|zhù hè}{你们|nǐ men}{获奖|huò jiǎng}！ |

~~{祝贺|zhù hè}{你|nǐ}{生日|shēng rì}{快乐|kuài lè}~~ mixes them up: a birthday wish is {祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{生日|shēng rì}{快乐|kuài lè}. {祝贺|zhù hè} is also used alone, as a
noun: {谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{祝贺|zhù hè} (thank you for your congratulations).

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 输 ✎ (traditional 輸) | to lose; to transport | shū | 车 | 13 | {输|shū} (lesson 04) |
| 组 ✎ (traditional 組) | group | zǔ | 纟 | 8 | {组|zǔ}, {小组|xiǎo zǔ} (lesson 04) |
| 项 (traditional 項) | item | xiàng | 页 | 9 | {项|xiàng} (lesson 04) |
| 邀 | to invite | yāo | 辶 | 16 | {邀请|yāo qǐng} (lesson 04) |
| 赢 (traditional 贏) | to win | yíng | 贝 | 17 | {赢|yíng}, {赢得|yíng dé} (lesson 04) |

  {组|zǔ} zǔ is 纟 + {且|qiě}, the {且|qiě} of {姐|jiě} jiě and {租|zū} zū (to rent, lesson 10): related sounds. {项|xiàng} xiàng is {工|gōng} +
  {页|yè}: {工|gōng} gōng also gives {江|jiāng} jiāng (a river, lesson 18) its sound; here it has drifted. {输|shū} shū is {车|chē} +
  {俞|yú}, the {俞|yú} of {愉|yú} yú ({愉快|yú kuài}, lesson 23): drifted. {申|shēn} shēn gives the sound of {神|shén} shén and {伸|shēn} shēn (later
  words). {标|biāo} biāo: in traditional {標|biāo}, {票|piào} piào gives the sound; simplified {标|biāo} has {示|shì} instead, which
  doesn't.

  in both it no longer gives a usable sound.

  only at the top, {甲|jiǎ} jiǎ only at the bottom, and {电|diàn} diàn turns into a hook. {失|shī} shī is {夫|fū} with its
  first stroke poking out at the top left; {先|xiān} xiān ({先生|xiān sheng}) has {儿|ér} at the bottom. {虑|lǜ} lǜ has {虍|hū}, the top of
  {虎|hǔ} hǔ (tiger, lesson 27), over {心|xīn}. {美|měi} měi is {羊|yáng} (its last stroke cut short) over {大|dà}. {梦|mèng} mèng is {林|lín} over
  {夕|xī} (evening), and {将|jiāng} has {夕|xī} too.

  left to right it's {亡|wáng}, {口|kǒu}, {月|yuè}, {贝|bèi}, {凡|fán}. Chinese schoolchildren learn it as those five parts.

### Stroke order

- **{毕|bì}**: {比|bǐ} first (a horizontal and a vertical with a rising tail, then a left-falling stroke and the
  vertical bend hook), then {十|shí}.
- **{失|shī}**: the short left-falling stroke at the top first, then two horizontals, the long
  left-falling stroke and the right-falling stroke.
- **{申|shēn}**: the left vertical, the top-and-right stroke, two horizontals, then the long vertical
  through the middle last.
- **{将|jiāng}**: 丬 (a dot, a rising stroke, a vertical), then {夕|xī}, then {寸|cùn} (a horizontal, the vertical hook,
  the dot).
- **{划|huà}**: {戈|gē} first (the horizontal, the long slanting hook, the left-falling stroke, the dot), then 刂.
- **{美|měi}**: a dot and a short left-falling stroke on top, two horizontals, the short vertical, the
  third horizontal, then {大|dà}.
- **{弃|qì}**: a dot and a horizontal, 厶 (a stroke that goes down and turns, a dot), then 廾 (a horizontal,
  a left-falling stroke, a vertical).

<summary>Model answers</summary>

- {我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{为了|wèi le}{工作|gōng zuò}，{而是|ér shì}{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{中国|Zhōng guó}{文化|wén huà}。 — I'm not learning Chinese for work, but
  because I like Chinese culture.
- {今后|jīn hòu}{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{都|dōu}{要|yào}{读|dú}{一|yì}{篇|piān}{中文|Zhōng wén}{文章|wén zhāng}。 — From now on I'm going to read a Chinese article every day.
- {我|wǒ}{今年|jīn nián}{的|de}{目标|mù biāo}{是|shì}{通过|tōng guò} HSK {四级|sì jí}。 — My goal this year is to pass HSK 4.
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Graduation
{祝贺|zhù hè}{你们|nǐ men}{毕业|bì yè}{了|le}！
= Congratulations on graduating!
{毕业|bì yè}{以后|yǐ hòu}{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}{计划|jì huà}？
= What are your plans after graduating?
{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{而是|ér shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}。
= It isn't that I don't want to go: I don't have time.
{我|wǒ}{的|de}{理想|lǐ xiǎng}{是|shì}{当|dāng}{一|yì}{名|míng}{记者|jì zhě}。
= My dream is to be a journalist.
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{英国|Yīng guó}{读|dú}{硕士|shuò shì}。
= I'd like to do a master's in Britain.
{不|bú}{要|yào}{放弃|fàng qì}！
= Don't give up!
{祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{一切|yí qiè}{顺利|shùn lì}！
= All the best!
```

## Pronunciation

- {将|jiāng} is jiāng in {将|jiāng}, {将要|jiāng yào} and {将来|jiāng lái}, first tone. (It has another reading, jiàng, "a general", that you
  won't need at this level.)
- {而|ér} ér is the same syllable as {儿|ér} ér and {而且|ér qiě} ér qiě; {而是|ér shì} ér shì.
- {硕士|shuò shì} shuò shì and {博士|bó shì} bó shì: the {士|shì} is shì, fourth tone, like {是|shì}.
- {考虑|kǎo lǜ} kǎo lǜ: *lǜ* has ü, with rounded lips; don't say *lù*.
- {毕业|bì yè} bì yè, {一切|yí qiè} yí qiè and {一生|yì shēng} yì shēng: {一|yī} changes with the tone after it, second tone before
  the fourth tone of {切|qiè}, fourth before the first tone of {生|shēng}.
- {目的|mù dì} mù dì: {的|dì} is dì here, fourth tone, not the light de of {我|wǒ}{的|de}.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{他|tā}{毕业|bì yè}{大学|dà xué}{了|le}~~: {毕业|bì yè} takes no object: {他|tā}{大学|dà xué}{毕业|bì yè}{了|le} / {他|tā}{从|cóng}{大学|dà xué}{毕业|bì yè}{了|le}. (Formal writing
  has {毕业|bì yè}{于|yú} + the school, with the written {于|yú}, "at, from": {毕业|bì yè}{于|yú}{北京大学|Běi jīng Dà xué}.)
- ~~{祝贺|zhù hè}{你|nǐ}{生日|shēng rì}{快乐|kuài lè}~~: for wishes, {祝|zhù}: {祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{生日|shēng rì}{快乐|kuài lè}. {祝贺|zhù hè} is for something achieved: {祝贺|zhù hè}{你|nǐ}{毕业|bì yè}{了|le}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{就是|jiù shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}~~ for "it's not that…, it's that…": that's {而是|ér shì} (or {是|shì}). {不|bú}{是|shì}…{就是|jiù shì} means
  "either… or".
- {我|wǒ}{将|jiāng}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}，{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？ in a chat is grammatical but sounds like a news report: say {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}.
- {我|wǒ}{的|de}{目的|mù dì}{是|shì}{考|kǎo}{一百|yì bǎi}{分|fēn} is heard, but a score you aim for is a {目标|mù biāo}; {目的|mù dì} is why you do something.

## Key points

- {不|bú}{是|shì} A ，{而是|ér shì} B: not A, but B (a correction). {不|bú}{是|shì} A ，{就是|jiù shì} B: either A or B.
- {将|jiāng} / {将要|jiāng yào} + verb: will, be going to (written); {会|huì} / {要|yào} / {快要|kuài yào} in speech. {将来|jiāng lái}: the future; {今后|jīn hòu}: from
  now on.
- {而|ér}: while, whereas (contrast); and, yet (joining). Written.
- {一切|yí qiè}: everything, all ({一切|yí qiè}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}; {祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{一切|yí qiè}{顺利|shùn lì}).
- {计划|jì huà}, {目标|mù biāo} (a goal), {目的|mù dì} (a purpose), {理想|lǐ xiǎng}, {梦想|mèng xiǎng}, {人生|rén shēng}, {一生|yì shēng}, {美好|měi hǎo}.
- {毕业|bì yè} (no object), {研究生|yán jiū shēng}, {硕士|shuò shì}, {博士|bó shì}, {奖学金|jiǎng xué jīn}, {申请|shēn qǐng}, {报考|bào kǎo}, {高考|gāo kǎo}, {通过|tōng guò}.
- {成功|chéng gōng}, {失败|shī bài}, {放弃|fàng qì}, {继续|jì xù}, {改变|gǎi biàn}, {成为|chéng wéi} ({为|wéi} wéi), {考虑|kǎo lǜ}.
- {祝|zhù} + person + wish (the future); {祝贺|zhù hè} + person + event (achieved).
- New characters (simplified): {={输|shū}、{组|zǔ}、{项|xiàng}、{邀|yāo}、{赢|yíng}、{毕|bì}、{博|bó}、{弃|qì}、{计|jì}、{划|huà}、{将|jiāng}、{继|jì}、{续|xù}、{虑|lǜ}、{梦|mèng}、{标|biāo}、{申|shēn}、{失|shī}、{美|měi}、{硕|shuò}=}; fifteen differ in traditional.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Du Fu: two poems
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In HSK 2 you read {李白|Lǐ Bái}'s {静夜思|Jìng yè sī} (Quiet Night Thoughts). This lesson is about the other great poet of
the Tang dynasty, {杜甫|Dù Fǔ} (Du Fu), and two short poems that Chinese children learn by heart: a
**[[quatrain]]** ({绝句|jué jù}) of four seven-character lines, and an eight-line poem about rain in spring. Both
are written in classical Chinese, so the words don't always mean what they mean today. For each
poem you get the text with pinyin, notes on the words, a version in modern Chinese, and our own
English translation. The lesson ends with a short modern text about Du Fu's life.

## Du Fu (712–770)

Du Fu lived from 712 to 770, in the Tang dynasty ({唐代|Táng dài}). He failed the official examinations as a
young man, and in his forties the An Lushan rebellion drove him and his family from place to place.
Nearly 1,500 poems attributed to him survive. From the end of 759 he spent most of the next five years in
Sichuan, much of it in {成都|Chéng dū} (Chengdu), living in a simple thatched cottage ({草堂|cǎo táng}); these were some
of the calmest years of his life, and both poems in this lesson come from them. A reconstruction of
the cottage, {杜甫草堂|Dù Fǔ Cǎo táng}, is a well-known sight in Chengdu today.

Chinese readers call him {诗圣|shī shèng}, "the sage of poetry".

## {绝句|jué jù} (Quatrain), by {杜甫|Dù Fǔ}

The title {绝句|jué jù} is simply the name of the form: a poem of four lines. Du Fu wrote it as one of a set
of four quatrains, and it is known by its first line.

> **{绝句|jué jù}**
>
> {两个黄鹂鸣翠柳|liǎng gè huáng lí míng cuì liǔ}，
>
> {一行白鹭上青天|yì háng bái lù shàng qīng tiān}。
>
> {窗含西岭千秋雪|chuāng hán xī lǐng qiān qiū xuě}，
>
> {门泊东吴万里船|mén bó Dōng Wú wàn lǐ chuán}。

### Words

| Characters | Here | Modern Chinese |
|---|---|---|
| {黄鹂|huáng lí} | orioles, small yellow songbirds | {一|yì}{种|zhǒng}{黄色|huáng sè}{的|de}{鸟|niǎo} |
| {鸣|míng} | to sing, to call (of birds) | {叫|jiào} |
| {翠|cuì} | jade green, fresh green | {绿|lǜ} |
| {柳|liǔ} | a willow | {柳树|liǔ shù} |
| {一|yì}{行|háng} | a line, a row ({行|háng} is háng here, as in {银行|yín háng}) | {一|yì}{排|pái} |
| {白鹭|bái lù} | egrets, tall white water birds | {白色|bái sè}{的|de}{鸟|niǎo} |
| {上|shàng}{青|qīng}{天|tiān} | to rise into the blue sky | {飞|fēi}{上|shàng}{蓝|lán}{天|tiān} |
| {窗|chuāng}{含|hán} | the window holds, frames ({含|hán}: to hold in the mouth, contain) | {从|cóng}{窗户|chuāng hu}{看|kàn}{出去|chū qù}，{能|néng}{看|kàn}{到|dào} |
| {西岭|xī lǐng} | the western ridge: the mountains west of Chengdu | {西|xī}{边|biān}{的|de}{山|shān} |
| {千|qiān}{秋|qiū}{雪|xuě} | snow of a thousand autumns: snow that never melts | {很|hěn}{多|duō}{年|nián}{都|dōu}{不|bú}{化|huà}{的|de}{雪|xuě} |
| {门|mén}{泊|bó} | at the door are moored ({泊|bó}: to moor a boat) | {门|mén}{外|wài}{停|tíng}{着|zhe} |
| {东吴|Dōng Wú} | Eastern Wu, the lower Yangtze, around today's Jiangsu and Zhejiang | {很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}{的|de}{东|dōng}{边|biān} |
| {万|wàn}{里|lǐ}{船|chuán} | boats of ten thousand li: boats that have come or will go a very long way | {从|cóng}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}{的|de}{地方|dì fang}{来|lái}{的|de}{船|chuán} |

### In modern Chinese

{两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{黄鹂|huáng lí}{在|zài}{绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{柳树|liǔ shù}{上|shàng}{叫|jiào}，{一|yì}{排|pái}{白鹭|bái lù}{飞|fēi}{上|shàng}{了|le}{蓝|lán}{天|tiān}。{从|cóng}{窗户|chuāng hu}{看|kàn}{出去|chū qù}，{能|néng}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{西|xī}{边|biān}{山|shān}{上|shàng}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{年|nián}
{都|dōu}{不|bú}{化|huà}{的|de}{雪|xuě}；{门|mén}{外|wài}{的|de}{江|jiāng}{上|shàng}，{停|tíng}{着|zhe}{要|yào}{去|qù}{东|dōng}{边|biān}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}{的|de}{地方|dì fang}{的|de}{船|chuán}。

({两|liǎng}{只|zhī}: two, for birds; {窗户|chuāng hu}: a window, lesson 10; {化|huà}: to melt; {江|jiāng}: a big river, lesson 18; {停|tíng}{着|zhe}:
moored, lying at rest.)

### Our translation

> Two orioles are singing in the green willows;
>
> a line of white egrets climbs the blue sky.
>
> My window frames the snow of a thousand autumns on the western hills;
>
> at my door are moored boats bound for Wu, ten thousand li away.

The poem is a set of four pictures: two near and small (the birds), two far and large (the
mountains, the river). Each line is built like the one it pairs with: number + colour + bird in the
first two ({两|liǎng}{个|gè}{黄鹂|huáng lí} / {一|yì}{行|háng}{白鹭|bái lù}), and window / door, west / east, a thousand autumns / ten thousand
li in the last two.

## {春夜喜雨|Chūn yè xǐ yǔ} (Welcome Rain on a Spring Night), by {杜甫|Dù Fǔ}

> **{春夜喜雨|Chūn yè xǐ yǔ}**
>
> {好雨知时节|hǎo yǔ zhī shí jié}，
>
> {当春乃发生|dāng chūn nǎi fā shēng}。
>
> {随风潜入夜|suí fēng qián rù yè}，
>
> {润物细无声|rùn wù xì wú shēng}。
>
> {野径云俱黑|yě jìng yún jù hēi}，
>
> {江船火独明|jiāng chuán huǒ dú míng}。
>
> {晓看红湿处|xiǎo kàn hóng shī chù}，
>
> {花重锦官城|huā zhòng Jǐn guān chéng}。

### Words

| Characters | Here | Modern Chinese |
|---|---|---|
| {喜|xǐ}{雨|yǔ} | glad of the rain | {为|wèi}{下雨|xià yǔ}{高兴|gāo xìng} |
| {知|zhī}{时|shí}{节|jié} | knows its season | {知道|zhī dào}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{该|gāi}{来|lái} |
| {当|dāng}{春|chūn} | just when spring comes | {正好|zhèng hǎo}{在|zài}{春天|chūn tiān} |
| {乃|nǎi} | then, and so (classical) | {就|jiù} |
| {发生|fā shēng} | to come forth, to bring things to life (not "to happen", its meaning today) | {下|xià}{起来|qǐ lái}，{让|ràng}{东西|dōng xi}{长|zhǎng}{起来|qǐ lái} |
| {随|suí}{风|fēng} | with the wind | {跟|gēn}{着|zhe}{风|fēng} |
| {潜|qián}{入|rù}{夜|yè} | slips secretly into the night | {悄悄|qiāo qiāo}{地|de}{在|zài}{夜里|yè li}{来|lái}{了|le} |
| {润|rùn}{物|wù} | moistens all things | {让|ràng}{东西|dōng xi}{变|biàn}{湿|shī} |
| {细|xì}{无|wú}{声|shēng} | finely, without a sound | {很|hěn}{细|xì}，{没有|méi yǒu}{声音|shēng yīn} |
| {野|yě}{径|jìng} | country paths | {野外|yě wài}{的|de}{小路|xiǎo lù} |
| {云|yún}{俱|jù}{黑|hēi} | the clouds are all black | {云|yún}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{黑|hēi}{的|de} |
| {火|huǒ}{独|dú}{明|míng} | only the lamps are bright | {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{灯|dēng}{是|shì}{亮|liàng}{的|de} |
| {晓|xiǎo}{看|kàn} | look at dawn | {早上|zǎo shang}{去|qù}{看|kàn} |
| {红|hóng}{湿|shī}{处|chù} | where it is red and wet: the wet flowers | {湿|shī}{了|le}{的|de}{红|hóng}{花|huā} |
| {花|huā}{重|zhòng} | the flowers are heavy (with rain) | {花|huā}{湿|shī}{了|le}，{变|biàn}{得|de}{很|hěn}{重|zhòng} |
| {锦官城|Jǐn guān chéng} | Jinguan City, the City of the Brocade Official: Chengdu | {成都|Chéng dū} |

Two readings to watch: {重|zhòng} is zhòng (heavy), as in {重要|zhòng yào}, not the chóng of lesson 02; and {处|chù} is chù
(a place), as in {到处|dào chù}. Chengdu was called {锦官城|Jǐn guān chéng} because in the Han dynasty an official there
oversaw the city's famous brocade ({锦|jǐn}, a richly woven silk).

### In modern Chinese

{好|hǎo}{雨|yǔ}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{知道|zhī dào}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{该|gāi}{来|lái}，{春天|chūn tiān}{一|yí}{到|dào}，{它|tā}{就|jiù}{下|xià}{起来|qǐ lái}{了|le}，{让|ràng}{万物|wàn wù}{长|zhǎng}{起来|qǐ lái}。{它|tā}{跟|gēn}{着|zhe}{风|fēng}，{悄悄|qiāo qiāo}{地|de}
{在|zài}{夜里|yè li}{来|lái}{了|le}，{很|hěn}{细|xì}{很|hěn}{轻|qīng}，{没有|méi yǒu}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{声音|shēng yīn}，{让|ràng}{一切|yí qiè}{都|dōu}{变|biàn}{湿|shī}{了|le}。{野外|yě wài}{的|de}{小路|xiǎo lù}{和|hé}{天|tiān}{上|shàng}{的|de}{云|yún}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{黑|hēi}
{的|de}，{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{江|jiāng}{上|shàng}{船|chuán}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{灯|dēng}{是|shì}{亮|liàng}{的|de}。{早上|zǎo shang}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{那些|nà xiē}{湿|shī}{了|le}{的|de}{红|hóng}{花|huā}{吧|ba}：{成都|Chéng dū}{城|chéng}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{花|huā}{带|dài}{着|zhe}{雨水|yǔ shuǐ}，{又|yòu}{重|zhòng}{又|yòu}
{美|měi}。

({该|gāi}: should, HSK 3; {万物|wàn wù}: all things; {长|zhǎng}{起来|qǐ lái}: to grow; {悄悄|qiāo qiāo}{地|de}: quietly, secretly; {夜里|yè li}: at
night; {轻|qīng}: light, gentle; {亮|liàng}: bright, lit; {野外|yě wài}: the open country; {雨水|yǔ shuǐ}: rainwater; {灯|dēng}: a lamp, HSK 3; {城|chéng}: a city,
lesson 18.)

### Our translation

> A good rain knows its season:
>
> just as spring arrives, it comes and brings things to life.
>
> It slips in with the wind by night,
>
> and softens everything, fine and without a sound.
>
> Over the country paths the clouds are all black;
>
> only a boat's lamp on the river shines.
>
> At dawn, look where the red is wet:
>
> the flowers hang heavy over the Brocade City.

The title's {喜|xǐ}{雨|yǔ} is rain that makes people glad: rain that comes when spring needs it. The poem never
says "I": it moves from the rain's arrival, to the dark night, to the morning, and lets the last
picture, heavy wet flowers all over the city, show the poet's joy.

## Du Fu and Li Bai

People talk about {杜甫|Dù Fǔ} and {李白|Lǐ Bái} together. {李白|Lǐ Bái} (about 701–762) was the older of the two; they met in
744 and became friends. Chinese readers call {李白|Lǐ Bái}{诗仙|shī xiān}, "the immortal of poetry", for his free,
soaring poems of wine, the moon and the mountains, and {杜甫|Dù Fǔ}{诗圣|shī shèng}, "the sage of poetry", for his care
with form and his poems about ordinary people's lives and the troubles of his times. Both {静夜思|Jìng yè sī} and
the two poems here are among the best-known poems in Chinese, and many children learn them by heart.

## Reading: Du Fu and Chengdu

A short text about Du Fu's life, in our own modern Chinese.

> **{杜甫|Dù Fǔ}{和|hé}{成都|Chéng dū}**
>
> {杜甫|Dù Fǔ}{是|shì}{唐代|Táng dài}{的|de}{诗人|shī rén}，{生活|shēng huó}{在|zài}{一千二百|yì qiān èr bǎi}{多|duō}{年|nián}{前|qián}。{今天|jīn tiān}{留|liú}{下来|xià lái}{的|de}{杜甫|Dù Fǔ}{的|de}{诗|shī}{有|yǒu}{将近|jiāng jìn}{一千五百|yì qiān wǔ bǎi}{首|shǒu}。
>
> {杜甫|Dù Fǔ}{的|de}{一生|yì shēng}{很|hěn}{不|bù}{容易|róng yì}。{他|tā}{年轻|nián qīng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{想|xiǎng}{当官|dāng guān}，{可是|kě shì}{考试|kǎo shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{成功|chéng gōng}。{后来|hòu lái}{国家|guó jiā}{发生|fā shēng}{了|le}{战争|zhàn zhēng}，{他|tā}{带|dài}{着|zhe}{家人|jiā rén}{到处|dào chù}{走|zǒu}，{生活|shēng huó}{十分|shí fēn}{困难|kùn nan}。
>

New words, glossed: {留|liú}{下来|xià lái} (to remain, survive), {将近|jiāng jìn} (nearly), {困难|kùn nan} (hard, difficult, lesson 12), {当官|dāng guān} (to become an official), {战争|zhàn zhēng} (war), {十分|shí fēn} (very, lesson 18),
{年底|nián dǐ} (the end of the year, lesson 15), {座|zuò} (the measure word for buildings, lesson 18), {远处|yuǎn chù} (far away),
{风景|fēng jǐng} (scenery, lesson 18), {年纪|nián jì} (age), {喝酒|hē jiǔ} (to drink wine), {月亮|yuè liang} (the moon), {自由|zì yóu} (freedom), {普通|pǔ tōng}
(ordinary, lesson 11), {参观|cān guān} (to visit a place, lesson 18), {日子|rì zi} (days, lesson 21), {背|bèi} (to recite).

1. How long ago did Du Fu live, and about how many of his poems survive?
2. Why was his life hard before he came to Chengdu?
3. What could he see from the thatched cottage?
4. Why are Li Bai and Du Fu called {诗仙|shī xiān} and {诗圣|shī shèng}?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Over 1,200 years ago, in the Tang dynasty; nearly 1,500 of his poems survive ({将近|jiāng jìn}{一千五百|yì qiān wǔ bǎi}{首|shǒu}).
2. He failed the official examinations, and then war came and he wandered from place to place with
   his family ({考试|kǎo shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{成功|chéng gōng}…{发生|fā shēng}{了|le}{战争|zhàn zhēng}…{到处|dào chù}{走|zǒu}).
3. Judging from his poems, a river beside it, willows in front of the door, and snowy mountains in
   the distance from the window ({从|cóng}{他|tā}{的|de}{诗|shī}{来|lái}{看|kàn}…{从|cóng}{窗户|chuāng hu}{能|néng}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{远处|yuǎn chù}{的|de}{雪山|xuě shān}).
4. Li Bai wrote about wine, the moon and freedom: the immortal of poetry. Du Fu wrote about ordinary
   people's lives: the sage of poetry.

"**Du Fu and Chengdu.** Du Fu was a poet of the Tang dynasty who lived more than 1,200 years ago.
Nearly 1,500 of his poems survive today. Du Fu's life was not easy. As a young man he wanted to
become an official, but he didn't pass the examinations. Later war came to the country, and he
travelled from place to place with his family, in great hardship. At the end of 759 Du Fu came to
Chengdu. He moved into a simple thatched cottage in Chengdu. Judging from his poems, there was a river
beside the cottage and willows in front of the door, and from the window you could see the snowy
mountains in the distance. His years in Chengdu were some of the calmest and happiest of his life. Both
'Welcome Rain on a Spring Night' and the 'Quatrain' were written in Chengdu. In the spring of
761 a spring rain fell on Chengdu; that night Du Fu listened to the rain outside his window, very happy, and
wrote 'Welcome Rain on a Spring Night'. So when we read these
two poems, we seem to see the view from his window too. People often talk about Du Fu and Li Bai
together. Li Bai was older than Du Fu, and the two were good friends. Li Bai's poems often speak of
wine, the moon and freedom, and people call him the 'immortal of poetry'; Du Fu's poems often speak
of the lives of ordinary people, and people call him the 'sage of poetry'. Today Chengdu still has
the 'Du Fu Thatched Cottage', and many people visit it every year. Both these poems are famous,
and many Chinese children can recite them."
</details>

## Say it

Read each poem aloud, a line at a time, then the whole poem. Classical poems are read slowly, with
a small pause after the second or fourth character of each line.

```speak
# Two poems by Du Fu
{两个黄鹂鸣翠柳|liǎng gè huáng lí míng cuì liǔ}，{一行白鹭上青天|yì háng bái lù shàng qīng tiān}。
= Two orioles are singing in the green willows; a line of white egrets climbs the blue sky.
{窗含西岭千秋雪|chuāng hán xī lǐng qiān qiū xuě}，{门泊东吴万里船|mén bó Dōng Wú wàn lǐ chuán}。
= My window frames the snow of a thousand autumns; at my door are boats bound for Wu.
{好雨知时节|hǎo yǔ zhī shí jié}，{当春乃发生|dāng chūn nǎi fā shēng}。
= A good rain knows its season: just as spring arrives, it comes.
{随风潜入夜|suí fēng qián rù yè}，{润物细无声|rùn wù xì wú shēng}。
= It slips in with the wind by night, and softens everything without a sound.
{晓看红湿处|xiǎo kàn hóng shī chù}，{花重锦官城|huā zhòng Jǐn guān chéng}。
= At dawn, look where the red is wet: the flowers hang heavy over the Brocade City.
```

## Key points

- {杜甫|Dù Fǔ} (712–770), the {诗圣|shī shèng} of the Tang dynasty; {李白|Lǐ Bái} (about 701–762) is the {诗仙|shī xiān}.
- {绝句|jué jù}: a four-line poem; Du Fu's "{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{黄鹂|huáng lí}{鸣|míng}{翠|cuì}{柳|liǔ}" pairs its lines word for word.
- {春夜喜雨|Chūn yè xǐ yǔ}: rain that "knows its season" and comes silently by night; {锦官城|Jǐn guān chéng} is Chengdu.
- Classical words keep old meanings: {发生|fā shēng} (to bring to life), {泊|bó} (to moor), {乃|nǎi} (then), {俱|jù} (all), {独|dú}
  (only). Watch the readings {行|háng} háng, {重|zhòng} zhòng and {处|chù} chù.

lessons.title: How Chinese writing changed
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have now learned about a thousand characters, and with the switch at the top of the page you
can see each of them in simplified or traditional form. This lesson tells the story behind both: how
the oldest Chinese writing we know, scratched on bones more than three thousand years ago, became the
characters of today. It is a history of a script, told without judging any of its forms. You'll
meet the names of the main styles of writing ({甲骨文|jiǎ gǔ wén}, {金文|jīn wén}, {小篆|xiǎo zhuàn}, {隶书|lì shū}, {楷书|kǎi shū}), the ways the
simplified characters were made, and the places where each form is used now. The lesson ends with a
reading in modern Chinese.

## The oldest writing: oracle bones

The earliest large body of Chinese writing is the **[[oracle bone script]]** ({甲骨文|jiǎ gǔ wén}, "shell-and-bone
writing"), from the late Shang dynasty, roughly 1250 to 1050 BCE. The Shang kings' diviners carved
questions on tortoise shells and the shoulder bones of oxen: will it rain, will the harvest be good,
should the king go hunting. They heated the bones until they cracked, read the answer in the cracks,
and often carved the result too. About 150,000 inscribed pieces have been found, with some 4,000
different characters. The scholar Wang Yirong recognised the carvings as ancient Chinese writing in
1899.

Some oracle-bone characters are still recognisable pictures: {日|rì} is a circle with a mark inside (the
sun), {月|yuè} a crescent moon, {人|rén} a person seen from the side, {木|mù} a tree with branches and roots, {山|shān} three
peaks. But by the late Shang most characters were no longer pictures: the script was already a full
writing system, with characters for sounds and abstract ideas.

## Bronze, then the Qin standard

**[[Bronze inscriptions]]** ({金文|jīn wén}, "metal writing") were cast into ritual vessels and bells, mainly in the
late Shang and Western Zhou dynasties (about 1250 to 771 BCE). Their lines are thicker and rounder
than the scratched lines of the bones.

Over the following centuries, as the Zhou kingdom broke up into rival states, each state's writing
developed in its own way. In the state of Qin the forms grew gradually more regular and symmetrical,
into the **[[small seal script]]** ({小篆|xiǎo zhuàn}). When Qin unified China in 221 BCE, its seal script became the
standard across the whole country, along with Qin's weights, measures and coins (the honors lesson
15h1 tells that story).

## Clerical and regular script

Seal script is beautiful but slow to write, with long curving lines. Clerks who wrote all day with
brush and ink used quicker, flatter forms, and from these, between the Warring States period and
the early Han dynasty, the **[[clerical script]]** ({隶书|lì shū}) developed: square, broad characters whose
strokes are mostly straight, with a wide, flaring right-falling stroke. From clerical script on,
Chinese characters are built of strokes rather than drawn lines, and many look much as they do
today.

The **[[regular script]]** ({楷书|kǎi shū}) grew out of it between the Han and the Three Kingdoms periods, became
the main style in the following centuries, and reached its mature, classic form in the Tang dynasty.
Regular script is the script of print and of careful handwriting today. Both simplified and
traditional characters are regular script: the stroke names, the stroke order and the tracing pads
in this course all come from it. Faster handwriting styles grew up beside it, above all the
**[[cursive script]]** ({草书|cǎo shū}), in which strokes run together.

| Script | Chinese | When | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|---|
| oracle bone script | {甲骨文|jiǎ gǔ wén} | late Shang, about 1250–1050 BCE | thin, angular lines carved on shell and bone |
| bronze inscriptions | {金文|jīn wén} | late Shang and Western Zhou | thicker, rounder lines cast in bronze |
| small seal script | {小篆|xiǎo zhuàn} | Qin; the standard from 221 BCE | even, curving lines, tall and symmetrical |
| clerical script | {隶书|lì shū} | Warring States to early Han | flat, square, with a flaring right-falling stroke |
| regular script | {楷书|kǎi shū} | from the Han and Three Kingdoms; mature in the Tang | separate strokes: the script you're learning |

## Simplified and traditional characters

For many centuries the forms written in careful regular script were the ones we now call
**[[traditional characters]]** ({繁体字|fán tǐ zì}). Many simpler shapes were used in everyday
handwriting all along. In the twentieth century, to make reading and writing easier to learn, the
government of the People's Republic of China made such simpler forms the official standard:

- **1956**: the Chinese Character Simplification Scheme ({汉字简化方案|Hàn zì jiǎn huà fāng àn}) was published in January 1956,
  with a first group of simplified characters and components.
- **1964**: the General List of Simplified Characters ({简化字总表|jiǎn huà zì zǒng biǎo}) gathered them into one list of about
  2,200 simplified characters.
- **2013**: the Table of General Standard Chinese Characters ({通用规范汉字表|Tōng yòng Guī fàn Hàn zì biǎo}) set out the standard forms
  of 8,105 characters in three levels (3,500 common characters, then 3,000 and 1,605 more).

The **[[simplified characters]]** ({简化字|jiǎn huà zì} or {简体字|jiǎn tǐ zì}) were made in a few main ways:

| Method | Simplified | Traditional | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| a handwriting (cursive) shape made regular | {={书|shū}=}, {={车|chē}=} | {+{书|shū}+}, {+{车|chē}+} | from popular cursive forms |
| keeping only part of the character | {={飞|fēi}=}, {={习|xí}=} | {+{飞|fēi}+}, {+{习|xí}+} | the rest is left out |
| a simpler component | {={门|mén}=}, {={说|shuō}=} | {+{门|mén}+}, {+{说|shuō}+} | {=讠=} for {言|yán} on the left |
| a simple stand-in shape | {={对|duì}=}, {={汉|hàn}=} | {+{对|duì}+}, {+{汉|hàn}+} | {又|yòu} stands for a complex part (HSK 3 lesson 26) |
| one character for several | {={发|fā}=}, {={干|gàn}=} | {+{出发|chū fā}+} and {+{头发|tóu fa}+}; {+{干净|gān jìng}+} and {+{干活儿|gàn huór}+} | {={发|fā}=} for {發|fā} and {髮|fà}; {={干|gàn}=} for {乾|gān} and {幹|gàn} |

The last method is why this course's traditional switch needs care: one simplified {={发|fā}=} stands for two
traditional characters, {發|fā} in {出发|chū fā} and {髮|fà} in {头发|tóu fa}, so the app has to know the word to choose the right
one.

## Where each form is used

Simplified characters are the standard in mainland China, and they are also used in Singapore and
Malaysia. Traditional characters are used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau and in many overseas
communities. The two forms write the same written language, and their characters correspond one to one in
most cases. A reader of one learns to read the other
with some practice, and many people read both.

This course follows the mainland standard: it is written in simplified characters with mainland
pronunciation and vocabulary, and its traditional switch shows Taiwan character forms with the
same mainland words.

## Reading: the story of Chinese characters

A short text in our own modern Chinese.

> {不管|bù guǎn}{是|shì}{简体字|jiǎn tǐ zì}{还是|hái shi}{繁体字|fán tǐ zì}，{都|dōu}{是|shì}{同一|tóng yī}{种|zhǒng}{文字|wén zì}。{学|xué}{好|hǎo}{了|le}{一|yì}{种|zhǒng}，{再|zài}{学|xué}{另|lìng}{一|yì}{种|zhǒng}{就|jiù}{不|bú}{太|tài}{难|nán}{了|le}。{今天|jīn tiān}，{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{两|liǎng}{种|zhǒng}{字|zì}{都|dōu}{认识|rèn shi}，{在|zài}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{和|hé}{手机|shǒu jī}{上|shàng}，{也|yě}{可以|kě yǐ}{很|hěn}{方便|fāng biàn}{地|de}{换来换去|huàn lái huàn qù}。

New words, glossed: {之|zhī}{一|yī} (one of: {之|zhī} is lesson 21's written {的|de}), {刻|kè} (to carve), {乌龟|wū guī} (a tortoise), {壳|ké}
(a shell), {骨头|gǔ tou} (a bone), {圆|yuán} (a circle), {铸|zhù} (to cast metal), {铜器|tóng qì} (bronze vessels), {统一|tǒng yī} (to unify), {全|quán}{国|guó} (the whole country), {毛笔|máo bǐ} (a writing brush), {普遍|pǔ biàn}
(common, widespread: lesson 25), {一|yì}{笔|bǐ}{一|yì}{笔|bǐ}{的|de}{样子|yàng zi} (written stroke by stroke; {样子|yàng zi}: a look, lesson 22), {出现|chū xiàn} (to appear, lesson 20), {公布|gōng bù} (to
announce, to publish), {方案|fāng àn} (a scheme), {笔画|bǐ huà} (strokes), {海外|hǎi wài}{华人|huá rén} (Chinese communities overseas), {不管|bù guǎn}…{都|dōu}
(whether… or…: lesson 25), {另|lìng}{一|yì}{种|zhǒng} (the other kind; {另|lìng}: lesson 14), {换来换去|huàn lái huàn qù} (to switch back and forth).

The four characters in quotation marks stay as they are in either script: {書|shū} and {門|mén} are the
traditional forms, {={书|shū}=} and {={门|mén}=} the simplified ones.

1. What is the oldest Chinese writing we can see today, and what was written on it?
2. Why did clerical script take over from seal script?
3. When was the simplification scheme published, and what changed?
4. What does the writer say about learning the other form?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. The Shang dynasty's oracle bone script, over 3,000 years old: questions people wanted answered,
   carved on tortoise shells and ox bones ({把|bǎ}{想|xiǎng}{问|wèn}{的|de}{问题|wèn tí}{刻|kè}{在|zài}{乌龟|wū guī}{的|de}{壳|ké}{和|hé}{牛|niú}{的|de}{骨头|gǔ tou}{上|shàng}).
2. Seal script was beautiful but slow to write ({写|xiě}{起来|qǐ lái}{比较|bǐ jiào}{慢|màn}); in the Han clerical script became
   more and more common, and characters came to be written stroke by stroke.
3. In 1956: many characters got fewer strokes ({很|hěn}{多|duō}{字|zì}{的|de}{笔画|bǐ huà}{变|biàn}{少|shǎo}{了|le}).
4. They are the same writing system: once you know one well, the other isn't too hard ({学|xué}{好|hǎo}{了|le}{一|yì}{种|zhǒng}
   ，{再|zài}{学|xué}{另|lìng}{一|yì}{种|zhǒng}{就|jiù}{不|bú}{太|tài}{难|nán}{了|le}).

"**The story of Chinese characters.** Chinese characters are one of the writing systems with the longest
history in the world. The earliest characters we can see today are the oracle bone inscriptions of the Shang
dynasty, more than 3,000 years ago. At that time people carved the questions they wanted to ask on
tortoise shells and ox bones, for example 'Will it rain tomorrow?' Some oracle-bone characters look
like pictures: {日|rì} (sun), for example, is a circle with a dot in the middle. Later people cast writing
on bronze vessels: these are the bronze inscriptions. After the Qin unified China, the whole country
used one script, called the small seal script. Seal script is beautiful, but rather slow to write.
By the Han dynasty people were already writing with a brush. Writing seal
script with a brush was slow, and clerical script was much quicker. So by the Han clerical script was
more and more widespread, and characters slowly came to be
made stroke by stroke. Later still regular script appeared, and all today's characters are regular
script. In 1956 China published a scheme for simplifying characters, and many characters got fewer
strokes: {書|shū} became {={书|shū}=} and {門|mén} became {={门|mén}=}, for example. Today simplified characters are used in mainland
China, Singapore and Malaysia; traditional characters are used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau and by
many Chinese communities overseas. Simplified or traditional, they are the same writing system. Once
you have learned one well, learning the other isn't too hard. Today many people can read both, and
on computers and phones you can easily switch back and forth."
</details>

## Key points

- {甲骨文|jiǎ gǔ wén}: the oracle bone script of the late Shang (about 1250–1050 BCE), carved for divination;
  recognised in 1899.
- {金文|jīn wén} (bronze inscriptions, Shang and Western Zhou) → {小篆|xiǎo zhuàn} (Qin; the national standard from 221 BCE)
  → {隶书|lì shū} (Warring States to Han: strokes instead of lines) → {楷书|kǎi shū} (Han to Tang: the script of today).
- 1956 scheme, 1964 list, 2013 table of 8,105 standard characters: the simplified standard.
- Simplification methods: cursive shapes, keeping part, simpler components, stand-in shapes, one
  character for several ({={发|fā}=} for {發|fā} and {髮|fà}).
- Simplified: mainland China, Singapore, Malaysia. Traditional: Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau and many
  overseas communities. One written language in two forms.

lessons.title: At the doctor's: describing an illness, 死了 and 厉害
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In HSK 3 (lesson 05) you could say you were ill: {感冒|gǎn mào}, {发烧|fā shāo}, {头|tóu}{疼|téng}, {去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}. At HSK 4 a doctor
wants more than that. One of the level's set tasks is describing an illness to a doctor: where it
hurts, since when, how badly, and what you've already done about it. This lesson gives you the words
for the body and the clinic, and the grammar for "how badly":

- the **[[degree complement]]** with {死|sǐ}{了|le} and {得|de}{厉害|lì hai}: {疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le} (it hurts like mad), {咳嗽|ké sou}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai} (a bad cough);
- {恐怕|kǒng pà} (I'm afraid that…, probably), for news you'd rather not give;
- {千万|qiān wàn} (whatever you do…), for warnings;
- {及时|jí shí} (in time, promptly);
- {量|liáng} liáng (to measure: {量|liáng}{体温|tǐ wēn}, take someone's temperature).

Module 2 moves from the doctor's to keeping fit, cooking, shopping and renting a flat: everyday
life after graduation. At the end of this lesson you can explain your symptoms, follow a doctor's
advice and tell the story of an injury from start to finish.

## Telling the doctor what's wrong

A doctor asks three things, and a good answer covers each.

**Where?** Name the part of the body, then the feeling:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {鼻子|bí zi} | nose | {我|wǒ}{鼻子|bí zi}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}。 My nose is bothering me (blocked or runny). |
| {胳膊|gē bo} | arm | {我|wǒ}{的|de}{右|yòu}{胳膊|gē bo}{疼|téng}。 My right arm hurts. |
| {肚子|dù zi} | belly, stomach | {他|tā}{肚子|dù zi}{疼|téng}，{吃|chī}{不|bu}{下|xià}{饭|fàn}。 He has a stomach ache and can't eat. |
| {皮肤|pí fū} | skin | {她|tā}{的|de}{皮肤|pí fū}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 Her skin is lovely. |
| {血|xuè} | blood | {手|shǒu}{上|shàng}{出|chū}{了|le}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{血|xuè}。 My hand bled a little. |
| {头痛|tóu tòng} | headache; to have a headache | {我|wǒ}{头痛|tóu tòng}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai}。 I have a terrible headache. |

{痛|tòng} and {疼|téng} (HSK 2) both mean "to hurt". {疼|téng} is the everyday spoken word; {痛|tòng} is a little more
written and lives mostly in compounds: {头痛|tóu tòng}, {肚子|dù zi}{痛|tòng}, and later {痛苦|tòng kǔ} (suffering). In speech {头|tóu}{疼|téng} and {头痛|tóu tòng}
are both common.

**Since when?** Give the starting point with {从|cóng}…({开始|kāi shǐ}), or the length of time with {了|le}:

{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{开始|kāi shǐ}{咳嗽|ké sou}。 — I started coughing last night.

{我|wǒ}{咳嗽|ké sou}{三|sān}{天|tiān}{了|le}。 — I've had a cough for three days. (Duration + {了|le} at the end: "and it still goes on".)

**How badly, and what else?** That's the job of the grammar below, plus a few useful words:

- {咳嗽|ké sou} késou, to cough; a cough (the second syllable is light). {咳|ké} ké is the short form, often in
  {咳|ké}{得|de}…: {晚上|wǎn shang}{咳|ké}{得|de}{睡|shuì}{不|bu}{好|hǎo}。 (At night I cough so much I can't sleep well.)
- {难受|nán shòu} (feeling awful, unwell; also upset): {我|wǒ}{全身|quán shēn}{都|dōu}{难受|nán shòu} is "I feel terrible all over" ({全身|quán shēn} is next
  lesson's word). {难受|nán shòu} is how you feel; {难|nán} + {受|shòu}, "hard to bear".
- {严重|yán zhòng} (serious, severe): {你|nǐ}{的|de}{病|bìng}{不|bù}{严重|yán zhòng}。 (It's nothing serious.) It goes with illnesses, problems and
  mistakes, never with people: not ~~{他|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{严重|yán zhòng}{的|de}{人|rén}~~ for "he's a serious person" (that's {认真|rèn zhēn}).
- {正常|zhèng cháng} (normal): {体温|tǐ wēn}{正常|zhèng cháng}。 (Your temperature is normal.)
- {受伤|shòu shāng} (to be injured, get hurt): {他|tā}{打|dǎ}{球|qiú}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{受伤|shòu shāng}{了|le}。 It's a separable verb: {受|shòu}{了|le}{伤|shāng}, {受|shòu}{了|le}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{伤|shāng}.
- {情况|qíng kuàng} (the situation, how things are): {你|nǐ}{的|de}{情况|qíng kuàng}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ (How are you doing?, from a doctor.)
- {感觉|gǎn jué} (a feeling; to feel): {现在|xiàn zài}{感觉|gǎn jué}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ (How do you feel now?) {我|wǒ}{感觉|gǎn jué}{好|hǎo}{多|duō}{了|le}。 (I feel much better.)

## How badly: degree complements with {死|sǐ}{了|le} and {厉害|lì hai}

HSK 3 gave you the **[[degree complement]]** with {得|de} + a description: {他|tā}{跑|pǎo}{得|de}{很|hěn}{快|kuài} (he runs fast). Two
complements say "extremely" with a strong, spoken feeling, and they're what people actually use at
the doctor's.

### Adjective or feeling verb + {死|sǐ}{了|le}

{死|sǐ} is "to die" (you'll meet it as a word in lesson 27). Straight after an adjective, with {了|le}, it
means "to death", which is to say "terribly":

{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le}。 — My head is killing me.

{今天|jīn tiān}{热|rè}{死|sǐ}{了|le}！ — It's boiling today!

{我|wǒ}{饿|è}{死|sǐ}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。 — I'm starving: let's go and eat.

There's no {得|de} and no {很|hěn}: ~~{很|hěn}{疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le}~~, ~~{疼|téng}{得|de}{死|sǐ}{了|le}~~. It's an exaggeration, so keep it for speech and
casual messages, never for a written report. Most often the feeling is unpleasant ({累|lèi}{死|sǐ}{了|le}, {急|jí}{死|sǐ}{了|le}, {气|qì}{死|sǐ}{了|le}: {气|qì}, to anger, is lesson 23),
but friends use it for good feelings too: {高兴|gāo xìng}{死|sǐ}{了|le} (thrilled), {想|xiǎng}{死|sǐ}{你|nǐ}{了|le} (I've missed you so much).
With a verb that takes an object, the object can come between: {气|qì}{死|sǐ}{我|wǒ}{了|le}！ (That makes me so angry!)

### Verb or adjective + {得|de} + {厉害|lì hai}

{厉害|lì hai} lìhai means "fierce, severe". After {得|de} it says that something is very strong, usually something
bad: an illness, pain, weather, traffic.

{他|tā}{咳嗽|ké sou}{得|de}{很|hěn}{厉害|lì hai}。 — He has a bad cough.

{我|wǒ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{肚子|dù zi}{疼|téng}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai}。 — Last night my stomach hurt badly.

{外面|wài miàn}{风|fēng}{刮|guā}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai}。 — The wind is blowing hard outside.

Unlike {死|sǐ}{了|le}, {厉害|lì hai} needs {得|de}: not ~~{疼|téng}{厉害|lì hai}~~. {很|hěn} before it is optional ({疼|téng}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai}, {疼|téng}{得|de}{很|hěn}{厉害|lì hai}).

### {厉害|lì hai} on its own: "formidable"

{厉害|lì hai} is also an ordinary adjective, and then it's often praise: someone who is formidably good at
something, or strict.

{你|nǐ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{做|zuò}{了|le}{这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{菜|cài}？{真|zhēn}{厉害|lì hai}！ — You cooked all these dishes on your own? Impressive!

{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}{很|hěn}{厉害|lì hai}，{作业|zuò yè}{没|méi}{写|xiě}{完|wán}{谁|shéi}{都|dōu}{不|bù}{能|néng}{走|zǒu}。 — Our teacher is strict: nobody leaves until their homework is done.

Context decides: {他|tā}{的|de}{病|bìng}{很|hěn}{厉害|lì hai} (his illness is bad), {他|tā}{很|hěn}{厉害|lì hai} (he's very good, or very strict).

| Pattern | Strength | Register | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {很|hěn} / {非常|fēi cháng} + adj. | very | neutral | {很|hěn}{疼|téng}, {非常|fēi cháng}{疼|téng} |
| adj. + {极|jí}{了|le} (HSK 3) | extremely | neutral, often positive | {好|hǎo}{极|jí}{了|le} |
| adj. + {得|de}{厉害|lì hai} | badly, severely | spoken | {疼|téng}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai} |
| adj. + {死|sǐ}{了|le} | terribly, "to death" | spoken, strong | {疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le} |

## {恐怕|kǒng pà}: I'm afraid that…

{恐怕|kǒng pà} kǒngpà puts a guess, usually an unwelcome one, gently: "I'm afraid…", "probably…, I fear". It
goes before the verb phrase or before the whole clause:

{你|nǐ}{的|de}{体温|tǐ wēn}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{高|gāo}，{恐怕|kǒng pà}{得|děi}{休息|xiū xi}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}。 — Your temperature is a bit high: I'm afraid you'll need to rest for a couple of days.

{这么|zhè me}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{他|tā}{恐怕|kǒng pà}{不|bú}{会|huì}{来|lái}{了|le}。 — It's so late: he probably won't come now.

{恐怕|kǒng pà}{明天|míng tiān}{会|huì}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — I'm afraid it may rain tomorrow.

Don't use it for "be afraid of": that's {怕|pà} (HSK 3): {我|wǒ}{怕|pà}{打针|dǎ zhēn} (I'm scared of injections), never
~~{我|wǒ}{恐怕|kǒng pà}{打针|dǎ zhēn}~~. {恐怕|kǒng pà} is about a likely outcome, not a fear of something.

## {千万|qiān wàn}: whatever you do…

{千万|qiān wàn} qiānwàn (literally "a thousand times ten thousand") makes a piece of advice urgent: "be sure
to…", or with a negative, "whatever you do, don't…". It comes before {要|yào}, {别|bié}, {不要|bú yào} or {不|bù}{能|néng}, and after the
subject if there is one:

{你|nǐ}{千万|qiān wàn}{要|yào}{记|jì}{住|zhù}，{饭|fàn}{后|hòu}{吃|chī}{药|yào}。 — Be sure to remember: take the medicine after meals.

{千万|qiān wàn}{别|bié}{告诉|gào su}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}！ — Whatever you do, don't tell my mum!

{这个|zhè ge}{药|yào}{千万|qiān wàn}{不|bù}{能|néng}{多|duō}{吃|chī}。 — On no account take more of this medicine than you should.

It's only for advice, warnings and requests. In a plain statement it doesn't fit: ~~{他|tā}{千万|qiān wàn}{来|lái}{了|le}~~.
In numbers, {千万|qiān wàn} is still "ten million": {两千万|liǎng qiān wàn}{人|rén} (twenty million people).

## {及时|jí shí}: in time, promptly

{及时|jí shí} means "at the right moment, before it's too late". It's an adjective ({来|lái}{得|de}{很|hěn}{及时|jí shí}, came just in
time) and works like an adverb straight before a verb:

{有|yǒu}{问题|wèn tí}{请|qǐng}{及时|jí shí}{告诉|gào su}{我们|wǒ men}。 — If there's a problem, please let us know promptly.

{还|hái}{好|hǎo}{你们|nǐ men}{送|sòng}{他|tā}{来|lái}{得|de}{很|hěn}{及时|jí shí}。 — Luckily you brought him in time.

Two words you'll meet soon are close but not the same: {按时|àn shí} (on schedule, at the set time: {按时|àn shí}{吃|chī}{药|yào},
lesson 07) and {准时|zhǔn shí} (punctual, lesson 17). {及时|jí shí} is about not being too late.

## At the clinic: {量|liáng}, {打针|dǎ zhēn}, {体检|tǐ jiǎn}

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {量|liáng} liáng | to measure | {护士|hù shi}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{量|liáng}{了|le}{体温|tǐ wēn}。 The nurse took my temperature. |
| {体温|tǐ wēn} | body temperature | {他|tā}{的|de}{体温|tǐ wēn}{是|shì}{三十八|sān shí bā}{度|dù}。 His temperature is 38 degrees. |
| {打针|dǎ zhēn} | to give or have an injection | {我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{最|zuì}{怕|pà}{打针|dǎ zhēn}。 As a child I hated injections. |
| {体检|tǐ jiǎn} | a physical check-up | {公司|gōng sī}{每|měi}{年|nián}{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{做|zuò}{一|yí}{次|cì}{体检|tǐ jiǎn}。 The company has us do a check-up every year. |
| {护士|hù shi} | nurse | {护士|hù shi}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{这里|zhè lǐ}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。 The nurse told me to wait here. |
| {大夫|dài fu} | doctor (spoken) | {大夫|dài fu}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{病|bìng}{严重|yán zhòng}{吗|ma}？ Doctor, is it serious? |
| {院长|yuàn zhǎng} | head (of a hospital, college) | {医院|yī yuàn}{的|de}{院长|yuàn zhǎng}{也|yě}{来|lái}{看|kàn}{他|tā}{了|le}。 Even the head of the hospital came to see him. |
| {眼镜|yǎn jìng} | glasses | {我|wǒ}{的|de}{眼镜|yǎn jìng}{找|zhǎo}{不|bu}{到|dào}{了|le}。 I can't find my glasses. |

- {量|liáng} is liáng when it's the verb "to measure" ({量|liáng}{体温|tǐ wēn}, {量|liáng}{一下|yí xià}{身高|shēn gāo}: measure your height). As a noun,
  "amount", it's liàng, as in {少量|shǎo liàng} (a small amount, lesson 08) and {数量|shù liàng} (quantity, lesson 15).
- {大夫|dài fu} is read *dàifu*, with a light second syllable. It's the spoken word for a doctor, and what
  patients call one to their face ({大夫|dài fu}, …). {医生|yī shēng} (HSK 1) is the neutral word, and the one for your job:
  {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}, not ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大夫|dài fu}~~ (heard, but less usual). Said dàfū, the same characters are an old title for
  officials, so the reading matters.
- {打针|dǎ zhēn} is a separable verb: {打|dǎ}{了|le}{一|yì}{针|zhēn} (had an injection).

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| {研|yán} ✎ | grind; study | yán | {石|shí} | 9 | {研究生|yán jiū shēng} (lesson 05), {研究|yán jiū} (lesson 27) |
| {究|jiū} ✎ | investigate | jiū | {穴|xué} | 7 | {研究生|yán jiū shēng}, {研究|yán jiū} |
| {贺|hè} (traditional {賀|hè}) | congratulate | hè | {贝|bèi} | 9 | {祝贺|zhù hè} (lesson 05) |
| {切|qiē} | cut; all | qiè (in {一切|yí qiè}) | {刀|dāo} | 4 | {一切|yí qiè} (lesson 05) |
| {鼻|bí} | nose | bí | {鼻|bí} | 14 | {鼻子|bí zi} |
| {胳|gē} | arm | gē | ⺼ | 10 | {胳膊|gē bo} |

### Meat on the left: ⺼

Four of today's characters have ⺼ on the left. It looks exactly like {月|yuè} (moon), but here it's the old
form of {肉|ròu} (meat, flesh), and it marks parts of the body: {胳|gē}, {膊|bó}, {肚|dù}, {肤|fū}, and ones you know already, {脸|liǎn}
(face), {脚|jiǎo} (foot), {腿|tuǐ} (leg), {胖|pàng} (fat). The right-hand part often gives the sound:

- {肤|fū} fū: ⺼ + {夫|fū} fū (still an exact match). Traditional {膚|fū} is a different shape altogether: {虍|hū} on
  top, {胃|wèi} below, 15 strokes.
- {肚|dù} dù: ⺼ + {土|tǔ} tǔ (the vowel has stayed, the tone and consonant have moved).
- {胳|gē} gē: ⺼ + {各|gè} gè (lesson 01): almost a perfect match.
- {膊|bó} bo: ⺼ + {尃|fū}, the same sound part as {博|bó} bó ({博士|bó shì}, lesson 05).

### Sound parts

- {及|jí} jí is the sound part of {极|jí} jí (HSK 3's {极|jí}{了|le}) and {级|jí} jí ({年级|nián jí}), and, further off, {吸|xī} xī (to
  breathe in, lesson 28). The {说文解字|Shuō wén jiě zì} (an ancient character dictionary, about 100 CE) explains {及|jí} as a
  hand {又|yòu} reaching a person {人|rén}: "to catch up with", which is still its meaning in {来不及|lái bu jí} (not in time).
- {皮|pí} pí is in {被|bèi} bèi (HSK 3) and {破|pò} pò (broken, lesson 10): the b / p has stayed, the vowel hasn't.
- {恐|kǒng} kǒng: {心|xīn} (heart, feeling) below {巩|gǒng} gǒng, which gave the sound.
- {咳|ké} ké: {口|kǒu} + {亥|hài}. {亥|hài} is also in {孩|hái} hái and {该|gāi} gāi: the sound has drifted too far to help, so learn
  {咳|ké} as {口|kǒu} + the right side of {孩|hái}.
- {究|jiū} jiū: {穴|xué} (cave, hole) + {九|jiǔ} jiǔ for the sound. {贺|hè} hè: {加|jiā} jiā + {贝|bèi} (money, gifts): congratulating
  came with presents, and {加|jiā} once gave the sound.
- {切|qiē} qiè: {七|qī} qī + {刀|dāo} (knife). In {一切|yí qiè} (everything) it's qiè; as the verb "to cut" ({切|qiē}{菜|cài}) it's qiē.

### The other characters

- {鼻|bí} bí: {自|zì} on top (zì, self). The {说文解字|Shuō wén jiě zì} says {自|zì} was itself a drawing of a nose; when {自|zì} came to
  mean "self", {鼻|bí} was made for the nose. People still point at their nose to say "me".
- {针|zhēn} zhēn: metal 钅 + {十|shí}. Traditional {針|zhēn} has {金|jīn} (8 strokes) on the left.
- {嗽|sòu} sou: {口|kǒu} + {束|shù} + {欠|qiàn}; {咳嗽|ké sou} is the only word you need it for.
- {量|liáng} liáng / liàng: {日|rì} on top, then a long horizontal, then {里|lǐ}. Two readings: liáng (to measure, the
  verb), liàng (amount, the noun).
- {厉|lì} lì: {厂|chǎng} + {万|wàn}. Traditional {厲|lì} keeps {厂|chǎng} but has {萬|wàn} inside (15 strokes).
- {况|kuàng} kuàng: {兄|xiōng} (older brother) with the two-stroke ice radical 冫. Traditional {況|kuàng} has the
  three-stroke water radical 氵 instead: 8 strokes.
- {伤|shāng} shāng: 亻 + ⺈ + {力|lì} in simplified; traditional {傷|shāng} has a different right side, 13 strokes.
- {温|wēn} wēn: water 氵 + {日|rì} over {皿|mǐn}. Traditional {溫|wēn} has {囚|qiú} (a person in a box) where simplified
  has {日|rì}: 13 strokes.

### Stroke order

- **{及|jí}**: only three strokes: the left-falling stroke, then one stroke that goes across, down,
  across and sweeps left ({横|héng}{折|zhé}{折|zhé}{撇|piě}), then the long right-falling stroke.
- **{皮|pí}**: the top horizontal-hook first, then the left-falling stroke and the short vertical, then
  the {又|yòu}-like bottom (a horizontal that turns down to the left, then the right-falling stroke): five strokes.
- **{鼻|bí}**: top to bottom: {自|zì} (6), then {田|tián} (5), then the bottom (a horizontal, a left-falling stroke and
  a vertical): 14 strokes.
- **{肚|dù}, {胳|gē}, {膊|bó}, {肤|fū}**: ⺼ first (left-falling, the horizontal-turn-hook, two short horizontals
  inside), then the right side.
- **{恐|kǒng}**: {巩|gǒng} first, then {心|xīn} at the bottom last.

"**That injury.** One Saturday last month I was playing basketball at the university with a few
classmates. It was hot that day, everyone wanted to get going, and we didn't warm up first.

We'd been playing for over half an hour when I jumped for the ball, landed badly and hit the ground

too, and it bled quite a lot.

My classmates took me straight to the hospital next to the university. The doctor had a look and
said it wasn't serious, and luckily we'd come in time. A nurse gave me an injection, and the doctor
told me to go back and rest, and on no account to play again that week.

stopped hurting and was back to normal.

   the table. Word: {难受|nán shòu}
2. A nurse is putting a thermometer under a child's arm while the mother watches. Word: {量|liáng}
3. A doctor hands a man a box of medicine and holds up three fingers. Word: {千万|qiān wàn}

<details>
<summary>Model answers</summary>

- {他|tā}{肚子|dù zi}{疼|téng}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai}，{看|kàn}{起来|qǐ lái}{很|hěn}{难受|nán shòu}。 — He has a bad stomach ache and looks really unwell.
- {护士|hù shi}{正在|zhèng zài}{给|gěi}{孩子|hái zi}{量|liáng}{体温|tǐ wēn}。 — The nurse is taking the child's temperature.
- {大夫|dài fu}{说|shuō}，{这个|zhè ge}{药|yào}{一|yì}{天|tiān}{吃|chī}{三|sān}{次|cì}，{千万|qiān wàn}{不|bù}{能|néng}{多|duō}{吃|chī}。 — The doctor says to take this medicine three times a day, and on no account to take more.

Other sentences are fine as long as they use the word naturally and fit the picture.
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# At the doctor's
{大夫|dài fu}，{我|wǒ}{咳嗽|ké sou}{得|de}{很|hěn}{厉害|lì hai}，{已经|yǐ jīng}{三|sān}{天|tiān}{了|le}。
= Doctor, I've had a bad cough for three days.
{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le}。
= My head is killing me.
{护士|hù shi}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{量|liáng}{了|le}{体温|tǐ wēn}，{三十八|sān shí bā}{度|dù}。
= The nurse took my temperature: 38 degrees.
{你|nǐ}{的|de}{情况|qíng kuàng}{不|bù}{严重|yán zhòng}，{不用|bú yòng}{打针|dǎ zhēn}。
= It's nothing serious; you don't need an injection.
{恐怕|kǒng pà}{得|děi}{休息|xiū xi}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}。
= I'm afraid you'll need two days' rest.
{千万|qiān wàn}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{吃|chī}{药|yào}！
= Whatever you do, don't forget your medicine!
```

## Pronunciation

- {咳嗽|ké sou} késou: the second syllable is light. So is {胳膊|gē bo} gēbo, and {大夫|dài fu} dàifu (with dài, not dà).
- {量|liáng}: liáng for "to measure" ({量|liáng}{体温|tǐ wēn}); liàng for "amount" ({少量|shǎo liàng}, {数量|shù liàng}). The verb is the one you say at the
  doctor's.
- {血|xuè} is xuè in words and careful speech ({血|xuè} on its own, {出|chū}{血|xuè}). In everyday speech many people say
  xiě in a few phrases ({出|chū}{了|le}{点儿|diǎnr}{血|xiě}, chū le diǎnr xiě); both are heard. Write xuè.
- {千万|qiān wàn} qiānwàn: first tone, then fourth.
- {恐怕|kǒng pà} kǒngpà: third + fourth. The third tone is a low half-third before the fall.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le}~~: {死|sǐ}{了|le} already means "terribly"; drop {很|hěn}: {我|wǒ}{疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le}.
- ~~{他|tā}{咳嗽|ké sou}{厉害|lì hai}~~: {厉害|lì hai} as a complement needs {得|de}: {他|tā}{咳嗽|ké sou}{得|de}({很|hěn}){厉害|lì hai}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{恐怕|kǒng pà}{打针|dǎ zhēn}~~ for "I'm afraid of injections": that's {怕|pà}: {我|wǒ}{怕|pà}{打针|dǎ zhēn}. {恐怕|kǒng pà} means "I'm afraid that…
  (probably)": {恐怕|kǒng pà}{要|yào}{打针|dǎ zhēn} (I'm afraid you'll need an injection).
- ~~{他|tā}{千万|qiān wàn}{来|lái}{了|le}~~: {千万|qiān wàn} is only for advice and warnings: {你|nǐ}{千万|qiān wàn}{要|yào}{来|lái}！ (Be sure to come!)
- {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大夫|dài fu} for your own job is heard but less usual; say {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}. And say dàifu, not dàfū.
- ~~{他|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{严重|yán zhòng}{的|de}{人|rén}~~: {严重|yán zhòng} is for problems and illnesses; a serious, careful person is {认真|rèn zhēn}.

## Key points

- At the doctor's: where (body word + {疼|téng} / {不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}), since when ({从|cóng}…{开始|kāi shǐ}; duration + {了|le}), how badly.
- Adjective or feeling verb + {死|sǐ}{了|le}: "terribly", spoken ({疼|téng}{死|sǐ}{了|le}, {累|lèi}{死|sǐ}{了|le}); no {得|de}, no {很|hěn}.
- Verb or adjective + {得|de} + ({很|hěn}){厉害|lì hai}: "badly, severely" ({咳嗽|ké sou}{得|de}{厉害|lì hai}). {厉害|lì hai} alone: severe, or formidable.
- {恐怕|kǒng pà} + verb phrase or clause: "I'm afraid that…, probably". "Afraid of" is {怕|pà}.
- {千万|qiān wàn} + {要|yào} / {别|bié} / {不要|bú yào} / {不|bù}{能|néng}: urgent advice and warnings.
- {及时|jí shí}: in time, promptly ({及时|jí shí}{告诉|gào su}{我|wǒ}, {来|lái}{得|de}{很|hěn}{及时|jí shí}).
- {量|liáng} liáng {体温|tǐ wēn}: take a temperature; {打针|dǎ zhēn}, {体检|tǐ jiǎn}, {护士|hù shi}, {大夫|dài fu} dàifu (spoken "doctor").
- New characters: {研|yán} {究|jiū} {贺|hè} {切|qiē} {鼻|bí} {胳|gē} {膊|bó} {肚|dù} {针|zhēn} {咳|ké} {嗽|sòu} {恐|kǒng} {量|liáng} {及|jí} {厉|lì} {皮|pí} {肤|fū} {况|kuàng} {伤|shāng} {温|wēn}; handwriting: {研|yán} {究|jiū} {量|liáng} {及|jí} {况|kuàng} {温|wēn}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Keeping fit: 往往, 偶尔, 老是 and 睡着
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Last lesson took you to the doctor. This one is about staying away: working out, sport, sleep and
stress. The grammar is mostly about *how often* and *how much*:

- **[[frequency adverbs]]**: {往往|wǎng wǎng} (tends to), {偶尔|ǒu ěr} (occasionally), {老是|lǎo shi} (always, as a complaint), beside
  {常常|cháng cháng} and {总是|zǒng shì}, which you know;
- {至少|zhì shǎo} (at least) and {尤其|yóu qí} (especially);
- {按时|àn shí} (on schedule) and {好好|hǎo hǎo} (properly);
- {着|zháo} as a result: {睡|shuì}{着|zháo} (to fall asleep), {没|méi}{睡|shuì}{着|zháo}, {睡|shuì}{不|bu}{着|zháo} (can't get to sleep);
- {养成|yǎng chéng} + {习惯|xí guàn} (to get into a habit).

The words cover the gym and its coach, ball games and their fans, and the body at rest: lying down,
waking up and being sleepy.

## How often: frequency adverbs

A **[[frequency adverb]]** says how often something happens. Like other adverbs it goes after the subject
and before the verb. From most to least often:

| Adverb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {总是|zǒng shì} (HSK 3) | always | {他|tā}{总是|zǒng shì}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。 He always gets up at seven. |
| {老是|lǎo shi} | always (spoken, usually a complaint) | {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{老是|lǎo shi}{迟到|chí dào}？ Why are you always late? |
| {常常|cháng cháng} / {经常|jīng cháng} (HSK 2–3) | often | {我|wǒ}{常常|cháng cháng}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{散步|sàn bù}。 I often go for a walk in the park. |
| {往往|wǎng wǎng} | tends to, usually (a pattern) | {周末|zhōu mò}{他|tā}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{去|qù}{爬|pá}{山|shān}。 At weekends he tends to go hiking. |
| {偶尔|ǒu ěr} | occasionally, once in a while | {我|wǒ}{偶尔|ǒu ěr}{喝|hē}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi}。 I have a coffee once in a while. |
| {从来|cóng lái}{不|bù} / {没|méi} (lesson 01) | never | {他|tā}{从来|cóng lái}{不|bú}{运动|yùn dòng}。 He never exercises. |

### {往往|wǎng wǎng} is not just "often"

{往往|wǎng wǎng} sums up a pattern you've seen: "in situation X, Y usually happens". So it needs a situation,
and it looks back on experience:

{周末|zhōu mò}{他|tā}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{去|qù}{爬|pá}{山|shān}。 — At weekends he tends to go hiking.

{一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{累|lèi}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{往往|wǎng wǎng}{容易|róng yì}{生病|shēng bìng}。 — People tend to fall ill when they're tired.

{刚|gāng}{开始|kāi shǐ}{健身|jiàn shēn}{的|de}{人|rén}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{练|liàn}{得|de}{太|tài}{多|duō}。 — People who've just started working out tend to overdo it.

{常常|cháng cháng} is freer. It can be about the future, in a request or a plan, and it doesn't need a
situation. {往往|wǎng wǎng} can't do either:

{以后|yǐ hòu}{请|qǐng}{常常|cháng cháng}{来|lái}{玩儿|wánr}！ — Do come round often! (not ~~{往往|wǎng wǎng}{来|lái}~~)

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{常常|cháng cháng}{去|qù}{健身房|jiàn shēn fáng}。 — I'd like to go to the gym often. (not ~~{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{去|qù}~~)

A quick test: if you can add "as a rule" or "typically" in English, {往往|wǎng wǎng} fits.

### {偶尔|ǒu ěr}: once in a while

{偶尔|ǒu ěr} is the other end of the scale: it happens, but not often.

{我|wǒ}{平常|píng cháng}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{酒|jiǔ}，{偶尔|ǒu ěr}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 — I don't usually drink; just a little now and then.

{他|tā}{偶尔|ǒu ěr}{也|yě}{会|huì}{迟到|chí dào}，{但是|dàn shì}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}。 — He's late occasionally too, but rarely.

### {老是|lǎo shi}: "always", and you're fed up

{老是|lǎo shi} lǎoshi is spoken. It says "always", like {总是|zǒng shì}, but nearly always as a complaint, often with {怎么|zěn me}:

{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{老是|lǎo shi}{玩儿|wánr}{手机|shǒu jī}？ — Why are you always on your phone?

{这|zhè}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}{老是|lǎo shi}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{真|zhēn}{烦|fán}{人|rén}。 — It keeps raining these days: so annoying. ({烦|fán}{人|rén}: annoying; {烦|fán} is lesson 23's word.)

Use {总是|zǒng shì} for a neutral habit ({他|tā}{总是|zǒng shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{上班|shàng bān}). With {老是|lǎo shi} the listener hears the annoyance.

## At least, especially: {至少|zhì shǎo} and {尤其|yóu qí}

**{至少|zhì shǎo}** (at least) goes before the verb, or before the number it limits:

{每|měi}{天|tiān}{至少|zhì shǎo}{要|yào}{走|zǒu}{六千|liù qiān}{步|bù}。 — You should walk at least six thousand steps a day.

{我|wǒ}{至少|zhì shǎo}{等|děng}{了|le}{你|nǐ}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}！ — I waited at least half an hour for you!

**{尤其|yóu qí}** (especially) picks out one case from a group. Before a noun, it's usually {尤其|yóu qí}{是|shì}:

{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{运动|yùn dòng}，{尤其|yóu qí}{是|shì}{游泳|yóu yǒng}。 — I love sport, especially swimming.

{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{尤其|yóu qí}{是|shì}{晚上|wǎn shang}。 — Winters in Beijing are cold, especially at night.

Before an adjective or a verb, {尤其|yóu qí} alone is fine: {今天|jīn tiān}{尤其|yóu qí}{冷|lěng} (it's especially cold today), {他|tā}{尤其|yóu qí}{喜欢|xǐ huan}
{打|dǎ}{排球|pái qiú} (he particularly likes volleyball).

## On schedule, and properly: {按时|àn shí} and {好好|hǎo hǎo}

**{按时|àn shí}** àn shí is "at the set time, on schedule": {按时|àn shí}{吃|chī}{药|yào} (take your medicine at the right times),
{按时|àn shí}{睡觉|shuì jiào} (go to bed at a regular time), {按时|àn shí}{交|jiāo}{作业|zuò yè} (hand homework in on time). Last lesson's {及时|jí shí}
was "in time, before it's too late"; {按时|àn shí} is "at the time that was set".

**{好好|hǎo hǎo}** hǎohǎo (in Beijing speech often hǎohāor, written {好好儿|hǎo hāor}) before a verb means "properly, as you
should":

{你|nǐ}{病|bìng}{了|le}，{要|yào}{好好|hǎo hǎo}{休息|xiū xi}。 — You're ill: you need a proper rest.

{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{好好|hǎo hǎo}{想想|xiǎng xiang}。 — Let's think this through properly.

## Fall asleep: {着|zháo} as a result

You know {着|zhe} as the light particle zhe (HSK 2: {门|mén}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}, the door is open). Read *zháo*, it's a verb
with the sense "to touch, to reach", and after another verb it says the action succeeded. It's a
result complement, like {完|wán} or {好|hǎo} (HSK 3):

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {睡|shuì}{着|zháo}({了|le}) | to fall asleep (did fall asleep) |
| {没|méi}{睡|shuì}{着|zháo} | didn't get to sleep |
| {睡|shuì}{得|de}{着|zháo} / {睡|shuì}{不|bu}{着|zháo} | can / can't get to sleep (potential) |
| {找|zhǎo}{着|zháo}({了|le}) | found it (= {找|zhǎo}{到|dào}) |

{孩子|hái zi}{已经|yǐ jīng}{睡|shuì}{着|zháo}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{小|xiǎo}{声|shēng}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 — The child's asleep now: let's keep our voices down.

{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{一直|yì zhí}{没|méi}{睡|shuì}{着|zháo}。 — I couldn't get to sleep at all last night.

{喝|hē}{了|le}{咖啡|kā fēi}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{睡|shuì}{不|bu}{着|zháo}。 — When I've had coffee I can't sleep.

{睡觉|shuì jiào} is the action of sleeping; {睡|shuì}{着|zháo} is the moment you drop off. So {我|wǒ}{十一|shí yī}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{了|le}，{一|yī}{点|diǎn}{才|cái}{睡|shuì}{着|zháo} is
"I went to bed at eleven but didn't fall asleep until one". {小|xiǎo}{声|shēng} (in a low voice) is {小|xiǎo} + {声|shēng} (sound).

{着|zháo} comes back in {着火|zháo huǒ} (to catch fire, lesson 10). In traditional characters both readings are
written {=著=}.

## Getting into a habit: {养成|yǎng chéng}

{养|yǎng} is "to raise, to keep" (HSK 3: {养|yǎng}{猫|māo}); {养成|yǎng chéng} is "to raise until it's formed", and its object is almost
always {习惯|xí guàn} (a habit):

{他|tā}{养成|yǎng chéng}{了|le}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{跑步|pǎo bù}{的|de}{习惯|xí guàn}。 — He's got into the habit of running every day.

{好|hǎo}{习惯|xí guàn}{要|yào}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{养成|yǎng chéng}。 — Good habits have to be formed from childhood.

The opposite, "to break a habit", is {改|gǎi}{掉|diào}{习惯|xí guàn} ({改|gǎi}, to change, lesson 02 + {掉|diào}, off, lesson 20).

## Working out

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {健身|jiàn shēn} | to work out, keep fit | {我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{健身|jiàn shēn}{三|sān}{次|cì}。 I work out three times a week. |
| {健身房|jiàn shēn fáng} | gym | {公司|gōng sī}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{健身房|jiàn shēn fáng}。 There's a gym next to the company. |
| {教练|jiào liàn} | coach, trainer | {教练|jiào liàn}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{先|xiān}{跑|pǎo}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。 The trainer had me run for ten minutes first. |
| {动作|dòng zuò} | movement, action | {这个|zhè ge}{动作|dòng zuò}{不|bù}{难|nán}，{你|nǐ}{试试|shì shi}。 This movement isn't hard: try it. |
| {力气|lì qi} | physical strength | {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{力气|lì qi}{了|le}。 I've got no strength left. |
| {体重|tǐ zhòng} | body weight | {他|tā}{的|de}{体重|tǐ zhòng}{是|shì}{七十|qī shí}{公斤|gōng jīn}。 He weighs seventy kilos. |
| {重|zhòng} / {轻|qīng} | heavy / light | {这个|zhè ge}{箱子|xiāng zi}{太|tài}{重|zhòng}{了|le}，{那个|nà ge}{很|hěn}{轻|qīng}。 This box is too heavy; that one's light. |
| {全身|quán shēn} / {身|shēn} | the whole body / body | {跑|pǎo}{完|wán}{步|bù}，{我|wǒ}{全身|quán shēn}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{汗|hàn}。 After running I was sweating all over. |
| {汗|hàn} | sweat | {他|tā}{出|chū}{了|le}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{汗|hàn}。 He sweated a lot. |
| {散步|sàn bù} / {步|bù} | to go for a walk / step | {晚饭|wǎn fàn}{以后|yǐ hòu}{去|qù}{散散步|sàn san bù}{吧|ba}。 Let's go for a walk after dinner. {每|měi}{天|tiān}{走|zǒu}{一万|yí wàn}{步|bù}。 Ten thousand steps a day. |
| {放松|fàng sōng} | to relax | {周末|zhōu mò}{要|yào}{好好|hǎo hǎo}{放松|fàng sōng}{一下|yí xià}。 You need to relax properly at the weekend. |
| {轻松|qīng sōng} | relaxed, easy | {考|kǎo}{完|wán}{试|shì}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{轻松|qīng sōng}。 After the exam everyone was relaxed. |
| {压力|yā lì} / {压|yā} | pressure, stress / to press | {工作|gōng zuò}{压力|yā lì}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。 There's a lot of pressure at work. {别|bié}{压|yā}{着|zhe}{书|shū}。 Don't press on the book. |
| {效果|xiào guǒ} | effect, result | {这个|zhè ge}{药|yào}{效果|xiào guǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 This medicine works well. |
| {功夫|gōng fu} | kung fu; skill, effort | {他|tā}{会|huì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{功夫|gōng fu}。 He knows kung fu. {下功夫|xià gōng fu} to put in the effort. |
| {日常|rì cháng} / {平常|píng cháng} | daily, everyday / ordinary; usually | {日常|rì cháng}{生活|shēng huó} daily life. {我|wǒ}{平常|píng cháng}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。 I usually get up at seven. |
| {早晨|zǎo chén} | early morning | {早晨|zǎo chén}{的|de}{公园|gōng yuán}{里|lǐ}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 The park is busy early in the morning. |

- {散步|sàn bù} is separable, and its verb doubles as {散散步|sàn san bù} (have a little walk): HSK 3's {走走|zǒu zou} is close. {步|bù} alone
  is a step, a pace: {一万|yí wàn}{步|bù}, {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}{两|liǎng}{步|bù} (take two steps forward).
- {汗|hàn} is counted with a borrowed measure word in {一|yì}{身|shēn}{汗|hàn} (a whole body of sweat: sweating all over),
  which is lesson 08's topic. {出|chū}{汗|hàn} is "to sweat".

### Meaning parts

- 疒 (sickness; traditionally explained as a sick person leaning on a bed) is in {病|bìng} and {疼|téng}, and now {痛|tòng}.
- 酉 was a wine jar: {酒|jiǔ} (wine), {醉|zuì} (drunk), and {醒|xǐng}, which the old dictionaries gloss as "to sober up";
  today it's "to wake". {酸|suān} (sour, lesson 08) has it too.
- 血 xuè: the {说文解字|Shuō wén jiě zì} explains it as a dish {皿|mǐn} (for offerings) with a drop of blood above it: the short
  left-falling stroke on top.

### Look-alikes

- 乒 and 乓 are mirror images: {丘|qiū} with one short stroke under it, a left-falling stroke on the left
  for 乒 pīng, a dot on the right for 乓 pāng. They only appear together, in {乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú}: the sound of the ball.
- 困 kùn ({木|mù} in a box) and {因|yīn} yīn ({大|dà} in a box, {因为|yīn wèi}). A memory aid: a tree boxed in can't grow,
  so it's stuck, worn out, sleepy.
- 汗 hàn (氵 + {干|gān}) and 汁 zhī (氵 + {十|shí}, lesson 08: {果汁|guǒ zhī}): count the horizontals on the right.

### Stroke order

- **血**: the short left-falling stroke on top first, then {皿|mǐn} (the vertical, the horizontal-turn,
  two short verticals, the long bottom horizontal last).
- **尔**: the left-falling stroke, the horizontal-hook, the vertical hook, then the left-falling stroke
  and the dot at the bottom.
- **压**: {厂|chǎng} first, then {土|tǔ} inside, and the dot last.
- **迷**: {米|mǐ} first, then 辶 last: the dot, the horizontal-turn-turn-left-falling stroke ({横|héng}{折|zhé}{折|zhé}{撇|piě}), and the
  long flat sweep.
